title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADR Process
author: Aisha Malik
content:
Purpose

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance, and our ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineering teams when designing new services, modifying serving behavior, or proposing architecture changes.

Scope

Applies to: all backend services, inference runtimes, SDKs, control planes, and infra-as-code managed resources. Does not replace team-level playbooks; instead it provides company-wide minimums and recommended practices.

Principles (high level)

- Developer-first: APIs and infra should prioritize predictable developer experience and safety for production deployments.
- Observable by default: Services must emit meaningful metrics, structured logs, and traces.
- Production-first: Design for SLOs (availability, latency) and graceful degradation.
- Reproducible infra: All provisioning must be expressed in IaC and reviewed.
- Incremental rollout: Model and code changes use canary / staged rollouts with clear rollback paths.

1) API Standards

Goal: Stable, discoverable, and backwards-compatible interfaces for internal and external customers.

Requirements:

- Use RESTful resources or gRPC for service-to-service contracts. Public/SDK-facing endpoints should follow REST + JSON over HTTPS.
- Versioning: All public APIs must include a version in the path (e.g. /v1/...). Internal experimental endpoints must include /experimental/ in the path and be flagged in API catalog.
- Idempotency: Mutating endpoints must support idempotency keys for retry safety.
- Pagination: Standardize on cursor-based pagination for large result sets.
- Errors: Return structured error objects with stable codes, human_message, and optional retry-after. Map HTTP codes to categories (4xx client, 5xx server).
- Security: TLS 1.2+ required; use OAuth2 or mTLS for service-to-service authentication depending on trust boundaries.
- Throttling: Implement per-route rate limits and return standard 429 responses with a Retry-After header.
- Contract tests: All SDK or external-facing APIs must include automated contract tests that run in CI.

API Design Checklist:

1. Define resource model and primary keys.
2. Design idempotency and retry semantics.
3. Include versioning strategy.
4. Add metrics for request count, error rate, latency p50/p95/p99.
5. Define SLOs and limit/quotas.

2) Coding Standards

Goal: Maintainable, reviewable, and secure codebases with consistent style across the organization.

Language & repo guidance:

- Primary languages: Go (backend control plane), Rust/C++ (performance-critical runtime), Python (evals and infra scripts), TypeScript (frontend & SDKs).
- Single responsibility: Prefer small services vs. large monoliths. If a service grows large, introduce clear module boundaries and ownership.
- Linters & formatters: Enforce gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, rustfmt/clippy for Rust, black/ruff for Python, and eslint/prettier for TypeScript. CI must fail on linter errors.
- Static analysis: Enable SAST checks (e.g. Semgrep rules tailored by security team) and dependency scanning in CI.
- Tests: Unit tests with minimum 60% coverage for new code; critical path code should have >80% and include integration tests in CI.
- Commit messages: Conventional Commits style (type(scope): subject). Example: feat(runtime): add dynamic kv cache eviction.

Code Review & Ownership:

- Require at least one approver outside the author\u2019s direct team for public API or infra changes.
- Changes touching runtime kernels, LLM execution paths, or quantization pipelines require explicit review from eng-serving-runtime.
- Long-lived feature branches must be rebased regularly and use feature flags for rollout.

3) Infrastructure Standards

Goal: Secure, auditable, and reproducible infrastructure that meets our SLO and compliance commitments.

IaC and provisioning:

- All cloud resources must be provisioned via Terraform (or approved IaC) stored in the infra repo. No manual console changes without a documented exception.
- Modules: Use shared modules for networking, IAM, and common platform primitives. Version modules and pin module versions in root stacks.
- Environment isolation: Separate accounts/projects for prod, staging, and dev. Network egress rules must be reviewed for private deployments.

Networking & security:

- Defense in depth: Use VPCs/subnets, security groups, and private endpoints for control planes and data plane separation.
- Secrets: Use KMS/HSM or managed secret stores (AWS KMS / Google KMS / HashiCorp Vault) with short-lived credentials where possible.
- RBAC: Principle of least privilege for IAM roles. Use policies scoped to resources and require automated policy checks.

Provisioning table (example):

| Resource Type | IaC Module | Required Tags | Owner Team | Approval Process |
|---------------|------------|---------------|------------|------------------|
| VPC / Network | network/vpc | team,env,project | eng-infra | PR review + infra-owner signoff |
| GPU Cluster   | compute/gpu | team,env,hw-class | eng-serving-runtime | Capacity review + security scan |

4) Model-Serving Standards

Goal: Predictable, cost-efficient, and observable model inference with safe deployment patterns.

Model lifecycle:

- Model catalog: Every model must have a catalog entry with id, architecture, weights-version, quantization-profile, input/output contract, and performance profile.
- Versioning: Use semantic model versioning (major.minor.patch) and immutable artifact storage (e.g. S3 w/ checksum).
- Compatibility tags: Declare compatibility (e.g. cpu-only, fp16-gpu, int8-compat) to allow automated routing and fallback.

Serving & rollouts:

- Canary policy: Start at 1% traffic, monitor errors and QoR metrics for 1-2h, then 10% for 3-6h before broad rollout. Automated rollback triggers on error rate spike (>2x baseline) or QoR regression above threshold.
- Fallback strategy: Define fallback model variants per route (lower-cost or lower-capacity variants) and an explicit degradation plan (e.g., shorten max tokens, reduce sampling temperature).

Performance profiling:

- Benchmark every model on target hardware with representative prompt sets. Collect p50/p95/p99 latency and tokens/sec at target batch sizes.
- Document recommended quantization profiles and expected quality deltas against float baselines.

5) Observability Standards

Goal: Minimize time-to-detect and time-to-resolve by standardizing signals and dashboards.

Signals required for all services:

- Metrics: request_count, http_request_duration_seconds{quantiles}, error_count, saturation metrics (cpu, gpu_util, mem), queue_depth, batch_size_distribution. Use Prometheus naming conventions.
- Traces: Instrument critical request paths end-to-end (client -> control plane -> runtime). Include trace ids in logs and API responses for support traces.
- Logs: Structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, service, env, request_id, trace_id, level, msg, error_code, latency_ms. Redact PII and secrets.

Dashboards & Alerts:

- Dashboards: Per-service overview (latency/error/throughput), per-model dashboards (latency by prompt size, tokens/sec), and platform health dashboards (cluster utilization, queue lengths).
- Alerts: Define alerts for SLO burn rate, increased error rates, sustained high GPU saturation (>85% for 10m), and queue growth. Alerting must include runbook link and suggested remediation.

SLO template (to be filled for each service):

- Objective: 99.9% availability for /v1/* control plane APIs measured monthly.
- Latency SLO: p95 < 200ms for control plane calls; model inference SLOs are model-specific and recorded in catalog.
- Error budget policy: Alert when monthly SLO burn > 10% and paging when > 50% burn.

6) Performance Standards & Benchmarking

Goal: Quantify cost/latency tradeoffs and ensure regressions are caught before release.

Benchmarks:

- Baseline workloads: Define small, medium, large prompt sets used in continuous perf tests. Run nightly benchmarks measuring tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies, GPU utilization, and cost-per-1M-tokens estimate.
- PR performance gates: Changes that touch runtime kernels or request paths require waterfall benchmarks in CI. Reject PRs with >5% regression in p95 latency or >7% regression in tokens/sec without mitigation plan.

Cost visibility:

- Track token-level cost breakdowns by model and route. Provide per-route cost dashboards and recommend batching/quantization suggestions to reduce unit cost.

7) Decision Records (ADRs)

Purpose: Record architecture decisions, alternatives considered, and consequences to ensure knowledge continuity.

ADRs must include:

- title, date, status (proposed, accepted, deprecated), authors, decision rationale, alternatives considered, and migration plan.
- Each ADR should be stored in the arch-adr repo and cross-linked to the relevant service page in Confluence.

ADR process:

1. Draft ADR and add to arch-adr repo as markdown following template.
2. Solicit feedback via reviewers in the owning_team and impacted teams.
3. Present at architecture review (bi-weekly) if the change impacts core runtime, infra, or public API.
4. After approval, update ADR status to accepted and create an implementation ticket with owners and timeline.

Existing notable ADRs (examples):

- ADR-2025-01: Runtime scheduling model (sharded KV + continous batching) - accepted.
- ADR-2025-08: Default quantization formats (int8-cg & fp16 fallback) - accepted.
- ADR-2025-14: Canary rollout thresholds and automated rollback triggers - accepted.

8) Approval & Exceptions

- Exceptions: Any deviation from these standards requires a documented exception request, a compensating control, and approval from eng-architecture and security (when applicable).
- Review cadence: This document is reviewed quarterly by eng-architecture; ADRs are reviewed monthly in architecture review.

Appendices

A: Example service-level SLO table

| Service | Availability SLO | Latency SLO (p95) | Error Budget Policy | Owner |
|--------:|------------------:|-------------------:|---------------------:|------:|
| api-control-plane | 99.95% | 200ms | Notify @10% burn, page @50% burn | eng-platform |
| text-generation-runtime | 99.9% | model-specific (see catalog) | Auto-scale + fallback on high burn | eng-serving-runtime |

B: Example API error response (JSON)

{
  "error": {
    "code": "model_unavailable",
    "message": "Primary model unavailable, falling back to reduced-capacity variant.",
    "retry_after": 30
  }
}

C: Rollout checklist

1. Create model/catalog entry and performance profile.
2. Add canary config and set 1% traffic.
3. Validate metrics (errors, QoR, latency) for 1-2h.
4. Advance to 10% and validate for 3-6h.
5. Full rollout and monitor for 48h.
6. Post-rollout retrospective and update ADRs/configs if needed.
